children.topic:
1. Embryology &
Surgical Anatomy

Embryological Origin: Develops during the
5th week of IUL from the dorsal mesogastrium
Parenchymal Composition

Red Pulp (75%): Blood sinusoids
and splenic cords

White Pulp (25%): Lymphocytes, monocytes,
macrophages surrounding central arteries.
Develops in the second trimester
Position & Dimensions

Located in the left hypochondrium,
protected posteriorly by ribs 9, 10, and 11
Long axis parallel to the 10th rib

Odd Numbers Mnemonic: 1 inch thick,
3 inches wide, 5 inches long.
Weight: 75-150 grams
Structural Landmarks

Ends: Tapering posterior (medial) end,
broad anterior (lateral) end

Borders: Sharp superior border with
a distinct notch. Smooth inferior border
Surfaces

Diaphragmatic: Smooth and convex,
related to the diaphragm

Visceral: Carries the hilum (splenic vessels
and tail of pancreas) and 4 impressions:
Gastric, Renal, Colic, Pancreatic

2. Ligaments, Peritoneum
& Vessels
Peritoneal Ligaments

Lienorenal (Splenorenal) Ligament:
Connects spleen to kidney.
Contains splenic vessels and tail of pancreas

⚠️ Surgical Alert: Pancreatic tail extends
into splenic hilum. Injury during splenectomy
causes hemorrhage, pancreatic fluid leak,
and subphrenic abscesses

Gastrosplenic Ligament:
Connects spleen to stomach.
Contains the short gastric vessels

Phrenicocolic Ligament:
Connects diaphragm to splenic flexure of colon.
Primary physical support for the spleen.
Directs splenic enlargement toward the right side
Vascular Anatomy

Splenic Artery: Arises from the celiac trunk.
Highly tortuous along the upper border of pancreas.
Divides into segmental branches at hilum,
making partial splenectomy possible

Splenic Vein: Runs along posterior surface
of pancreas. Receives the IMV at neck of pancreas.
Joins SMV to form the portal vein
Congenital & Acquired Anomalies

Accessory Spleens (Splenules):
Located at hilum (50%), splenic vessels/
pancreatic tail (30%), or splenic ligaments

⚠️ Surgical Alert: If missed during splenectomy
for hematologic disorders, they undergo
hyperplastic expansion causing recurrence
of the primary disease

Splenosis: Acquired auto-implantation
of splenic tissue in various body compartments.
Typically seen after abdominal trauma or surgery

3. Physiological Functions
(The Seven Pillars)

1. Hematopoiesis: Produces RBCs during
5th to 8th months of IUL.
Normally stops after birth

2. Immune Function: Produces IgM,
non-specific opsonins (Tuftsin and Properdin)
that destroy encapsulated bacteria and fungi,
and antiviral Interferon

3. Filtration (Culling): Captures and removes
abnormal platelets and senescent RBCs
from circulation

4. Filtration (Pitting): Strips particulate
inclusions (nuclei or malaria parasites)
from RBCs without destroying the cell

5. Platelet Pooling: Stores 30-40% of
body platelets. In splenomegaly, sequestration
increases to 80%, causing thrombocytopenia

6. Reservoir: Holds approximately 8%
of total red cell mass

7. Phagocytosis: Reticular macrophages
capture circulating cellular debris and bacteria,
particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae

4. Splenic Trauma
& Rupture
Etiology

Closed (Blunt) Trauma (>70%):
Direct blows to LUQ (MVA, sports injuries)
or indirect trauma from fractured lower
left ribs (9th-11th ribs)

Open (Penetrating) Trauma (<30%):
Direct laceration from stab or bullet wounds

Predisposing Factors: Malaria or
portal hypertension cause splenomegaly,
rendering spleen soft, friable, and vulnerable
to spontaneous or minor trauma

Pathology of Injury:
Subcapsular hematoma, superficial/deep tears,
avulsion of a pole, complete depulping,
or laceration of the vascular pedicle

Delayed Rupture: Subcapsular hematoma
or tear temporarily sealed by blood clots
or greater omentum. Retraction of clot/omentum
up to 2 weeks later causes sudden massive
intraperitoneal blowout

5. Clinical Presentation
(3-Stage Cascade)

A. Fatal Type: Sudden catastrophic hemorrhage
and immediate death from tearing of major
splenic vessels or complete avulsion
of the splenic pedicle
B. Classical Type (3 Stages)

Stage 1 - Hypovolemic Shock:
Weak rapid pulse, tachypnea (air hunger),
hypotension, hypothermia, pallor,
cold extremities

Stage 2 - Recovery (Lucid Interval):
Temporary stabilization and improvement
of BP due to transient clotting and
hypotension-induced slowing of hemorrhage

Stage 3 - Internal Hemorrhage:
Recurrent severe bleeding as resuscitation
restores BP, displacing temporary clots

LUQ Signs: Guarding, rigidity,
tenderness, palpable perisplenic mass

Kehr Sign: Referred pain in the
left shoulder due to subdiaphragmatic blood
irritating the phrenic nerve

Balance Sign: Fixed dullness on percussion
in left flank with shifting dullness in right flank.
Indicates large clotted perisplenic blood

Cullen Sign: Periumbilical blue-red
ecchymosis indicating tracking
retroperitoneal blood
6. Diagnostic Workup

Plain Abdominal X-ray:
Obliteration of psoas and splenic shadows,
indentation of gastric air bubble,
elevation of left hemi-diaphragm,
and/or fractured lower ribs

Contrast-Enhanced CT Scan:
Gold standard in stable patients.
Defines exact grading of injury and
detects active contrast extravasation (blush)

FAST (Focused Assessment with
Sonography for Trauma):
Initial screening modality to detect
free intraperitoneal fluid

Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage (DPL):
Reserved for unstable patients when FAST
is unavailable or equivocal

Positive if fluid returns bloody/pink,
contains >100,000 RBC/mL,
or >500 WBC/mL
7. Treatment Algorithm
A. Non-Operative (Conservative)

Indications: Hemodynamically stable
(SBP >90 mmHg, HR <120 bpm),
minor trauma (subcapsular hematoma/
low-grade tear), no peritonitis

Method: Strict bed rest, close clinical
observation, and serial CT scans

Interventional: CT contrast blush
indicating active bleeding requires
splenic artery embolization if stable
B. Operative (Surgical)

Indications: Hemodynamic instability,
failure of conservative therapy,
or associated hollow organ injuries

Splenectomy: Complete removal.
Treatment of choice for severe,
unstable, or shattered spleens

Splenic Preservation (Salvage):
Extremely important in children under 15
to preserve immune function
Splenorrhaphy (suture of tears)
Partial splenectomy (if one pole avulsed)
Mesh wrapping (tamponade the bleed)

Auto-transplantation of minced fragments
into the greater omentum

8. Post-Splenectomy
Complications & OPSI
Post-Operative Complications

Hemorrhage: Reactionary bleeding from
a slipped splenic pedicle ligature

Subphrenic Abscess: Secondary to
poor hemostasis or fluid accumulation

Fistulae: Gastric fistula (damage to
short gastric vessels) or pancreatic fistula
(injury to pancreatic tail during ligation)

Thromboembolism: Transient post-splenectomy
thrombocytosis (rising platelets)
and leukocytosis

Pulmonary: Left basal lung
collapse/atelectasis

Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy
Infection (OPSI / OPSS)

Highly lethal septicemia with
2% overall mortality risk

Causative Organisms:
Streptococcus pneumoniae,
Neisseria meningitidis,
Haemophilus influenzae
OPSI Prophylaxis Guidelines

Vaccination: Must cover S. pneumoniae,
H. influenzae type B (HiB),
and N. meningitidis

Timing: Ideally exactly 2 weeks
after surgery (to maximize immune response)
or prior to discharge

Antibiotics: Daily prophylactic oral
penicillin or amoxicillin.
Recommended for at least 2 years
in children following splenectomy
